description: Checks whether the candidate can handle customers professionally and effectively by phone, WhatsApp and in person.

competencies.name: Communication Channels and Etiquette
competencies.description: Using phone, WhatsApp and face-to-face contact in a polite, clear and professional way.

competencies.name: Empathy and Active Listening
competencies.description: Listening carefully and showing understanding of the customer's situation and feelings.

competencies.name: Problem Solving and Ownership
competencies.description: Taking responsibility for a customer's issue and driving it to a correct resolution or a proper hand-over.

competencies.name: Handling Complaints and Difficult Customers
competencies.description: Staying calm and professional with angry customers and applying policy fairly.

competencies.name: Follow-up and Service Standards
competencies.description: Keeping promises, following up and learning from repeated problems.

questions.text: A customer calls your school-software support line. What is the best way to begin the call?

options.text: Say 'Hello' and then wait silently until the customer has explained everything.
Greet the customer, say your name and company, and ask how you can help.
Ask the customer to send the problem by email instead of speaking to you.
Ask for the customer's account number before you say anything else.

questions.explanation: A clear greeting with your name and company is polite and builds trust. Then you ask how you can help.

questions.text: A parent sends a WhatsApp message at 8 pm asking about a fee balance. Your office closes at 5 pm. What is the best response?

options.text: Wait until Friday so that you can answer all of the week's fee messages together in one batch.
Guess the balance from last term's figures so that the parent is not left waiting overnight.
Reply briefly that you received the message and will give the balance tomorrow morning.
Phone the parent repeatedly during the night until the parent answers to give the balance.

questions.explanation: A short acknowledgement with a clear time for the answer manages expectations. Guessing a balance or disturbing the parent at night is unprofessional.

questions.text: What does active listening mean?

options.text: Thinking about your reply while the customer is still speaking, so that you answer faster.
Repeating the same sentence louder and more slowly until the customer finally agrees.
Writing down only the customer's name and phone number so that you can call back later.
Giving full attention, not interrupting, and checking that you understood.

questions.explanation: Active listening means focusing on the speaker, letting them finish, and confirming what you heard.

questions.text: A parent comes to the school office and shouts that the invoice is wrong. What should you do first?

options.text: Let the parent finish, show that you understand the concern, then check the invoice.
Tell the parent that the office never makes mistakes and that the invoice must be paid as shown.
Cancel the invoice immediately and issue a new one so that the parent calms down quickly.
Ask the parent to leave and come back later with another family member to discuss it calmly.

questions.explanation: Letting the person speak and acknowledging the concern calms the situation. You then check the facts before taking any action.

questions.text: You cannot solve a customer's problem and must pass it to a colleague. What is the best practice?

options.text: Tell the customer it is not your department and that they should call the main office again tomorrow.
Pass on only the customer's name and phone number and let the colleague ask everything again.
Explain who will help, share all case details, and say when the customer will hear back.
Promise that the problem will be fixed today without first checking with the colleague who will handle it.

questions.explanation: A good hand-over means the customer does not repeat the story and knows who will help and when.

questions.text: A school bursar says a parent paid by mobile money, but the system shows no payment. What is the best first action?

options.text: Tell the parent to pay again so that the system can update, and promise to refund the first payment later.
Ask for the transaction reference, amount and time, then check them against the payment records.
Say that the payment never happened because it is not in the system, and ask the parent to bring proof.
Record the payment as received without checking, to keep the parent happy and avoid a long argument.

questions.explanation: Verify the details first. Asking for double payment, denying the payment, or recording it without checking can all cause loss or disputes.

questions.text: Which actions help to calm an angry customer? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tell the customer to calm down.
Speak slowly and calmly in a respectful tone.
Point out immediately where the customer made a mistake.
Apologise for the inconvenience and explain what you will do next.
Listen without interrupting until the customer has finished.

questions.explanation: A calm tone, a sincere apology with next steps, and patient listening reduce anger. Telling someone to calm down or blaming them makes it worse.

questions.text: A school owner asks you to waive a setup fee, but company policy does not allow it. What is the best response?

options.text: Agree quietly now, and then ask your manager to approve the waiver later when nobody is watching the accounts.
Say you will ask your manager and promise the owner that the waiver will be approved by the end of the week.
Refuse and end the call straight away because the policy is final and cannot be discussed with anyone.
Explain the policy and its reason politely, offer what is allowed, and escalate if the owner asks.

questions.explanation: Explaining the policy respectfully, offering alternatives and escalating when asked is honest and keeps the relationship. Over-promising or ignoring policy causes bigger problems later.

questions.text: The same problem is reported by several schools every week. What is the best long-term action?

options.text: Find the root cause, record the pattern, and report it so that it can be fixed.
Give each school the same temporary workaround and keep closing the cases.
Tell the schools that the problem is known and they must wait.
Handle it only when a school complains loudly enough.

questions.explanation: Repeated problems need a root-cause fix. Closing each case with a workaround treats the symptom, not the cause.

questions.text: Why should you follow up with a customer after solving their problem?

options.text: To make the customer buy another product immediately.
To confirm that the problem is really solved and the customer is satisfied.
To keep the ticket open for longer on the system.
To avoid receiving more calls from the same customer.

questions.explanation: Follow-up confirms the solution worked and shows the customer that you care about the result.

questions.text: Which are good practices when giving support by WhatsApp? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep messages short, clear and polite.
Use slang and many abbreviations to sound friendly.
Do not share another customer's personal details.
Reply 'OK' when you did not understand the request.
Confirm that you understood the problem before giving a solution.

questions.explanation: Short clear messages, protecting other customers' privacy and confirming understanding make WhatsApp support professional.

questions.text: You promised a school to call back on Friday, but you still do not have the answer. What should you do?

options.text: Wait until you have the answer, even if it takes until next week.
Ask a colleague to say that you are not available.
Call on Friday as promised, explain the progress, and agree on a new time.
Send the answer later without any message on Friday.

questions.explanation: Keeping your promise to update, even without the final answer, protects trust and lets the customer plan.

description: Checks whether the candidate can onboard schools onto software, drive adoption, monitor account health and prevent churn.

competencies.name: Onboarding Planning
competencies.description: Setting goals, timelines and data preparation so that a new school starts correctly.

competencies.name: Training and Adoption
competencies.description: Training users by role and helping them to use the software regularly.

competencies.name: Customer Health Monitoring
competencies.description: Using usage and relationship signals to see which customers are healthy or at risk.

competencies.name: Retention and Churn Prevention
competencies.description: Acting early to keep customers, understanding reasons for leaving and handling renewals fairly.

competencies.name: Stakeholder Communication
competencies.description: Setting expectations and giving clear updates to school leaders and users.

questions.text: What is the main goal of onboarding a new school onto school-management software?

options.text: Collect the first payment as quickly as possible, before the school changes its mind.
Show every feature of the system in one long meeting so that nothing is left out.
Help the school use the key features correctly so that it gets value quickly.
Make sure the school never needs to contact support after the go-live date has passed.

questions.explanation: Onboarding exists to bring the customer to real value quickly. Payment, long demos and zero support are not the goal.

questions.text: Which activity should happen early in onboarding, before the main training?

options.text: Agree the school's goals, a timeline, and who is responsible for each task.
Send an invoice for next year's renewal so that the payment is arranged in advance.
Switch on all optional features for every user so that nobody misses anything later.
Wait until staff ask for training before planning anything, so the sessions match their needs.

questions.explanation: A shared plan with goals, dates and owners keeps onboarding on track from the start.

questions.text: A school has 800 student records in several Excel files with different formats and wants to go live next week. What is the best approach?

options.text: Import all files as they are to meet the go-live date, and correct any errors during the term.
Agree a standard template, clean and check the data, import it, and move the date if needed.
Tell the school that the software cannot work with Excel files and that it must retype everything.
Type all 800 students yourself from the files, without checking them against the original records.

questions.explanation: Clean, checked data is the base of a successful start. A short delay is better than wrong records for the whole term.

questions.text: Which training approach usually helps school staff to adopt new software best?

options.text: One long lecture about every feature of the system, given to all staff together in the school hall.
A long PDF manual sent to each person, who must read it alone before the system goes live next month.
Training only the headmaster, who then teaches everyone else in his own way when he has time.
Short sessions for each role, such as bursar and teachers, with practice on real tasks.

questions.explanation: Role-based, hands-on training lets each person practise the tasks they will really do.

questions.text: Three weeks after training, teachers at a school still record marks on paper. What should you do first?

options.text: Tell the headmaster that the teachers are resisting change and should be ordered to use the system.
Repeat the same full training once more without changing anything, since it worked well at other schools.
Ask the teachers why, for example about skills, devices or time, and then address the barriers.
Close the onboarding project because the training is complete and the school now has the system.

questions.explanation: Adoption problems have causes. Finding the real barrier lets you fix it instead of repeating what did not work.

questions.text: Which signals may show that a school is at risk of leaving? Select all that apply.

options.text: The main users have not logged in for several weeks.
The school asks for training for newly employed staff.
The school does not reply to your messages about the renewal.
The school uses reports from the system every month.
The bursar who championed the system left and nobody replaced them.

questions.explanation: Low usage, silence and the loss of a champion are warning signs. Asking for training and using reports are healthy signs.

questions.text: What is a customer health score?

options.text: A combined score of usage, support and relationship signals showing how likely the customer is to stay.
The total amount of money that the customer has paid so far, including setup fees and every renewal payment.
The average rating that a customer gives after each support call, on a scale of one to five stars, over a year.
The number of support tickets the customer has opened during the current subscription year.

questions.explanation: A health score combines several signals so that the team can spot at-risk and healthy accounts early. One number alone, such as payments or tickets, is not enough.

questions.text: A school's logins fell sharply this term and its renewal is in two months. What is the best action?

options.text: Wait until the renewal date is very close and then ask the owner whether the school wants to continue.
Offer a large discount immediately, before you have found out why the school's usage has dropped.
Send a general SMS about the renewal deadline to all customers and wait for this school to reply.
Contact the school now, find the cause, agree a recovery plan, and involve the decision-maker.

questions.explanation: Early contact, finding the cause and involving the decision-maker gives the best chance to recover the account.

questions.text: What does 'churn' mean in customer success?

options.text: New customers who sign up during a month.
Customers who stop using or paying for your service.
Customers who ask for extra training.
Staff who leave your own company.

questions.explanation: Churn is the loss of customers, either when they cancel or when they stop paying or using the service.

questions.text: A school says it will not renew because the fee is too high and it hardly uses the SMS module. What is the best response?

options.text: Agree and cancel the account at once, without asking any questions about the school's usage or needs.
Explain that all schools pay the same price, so the fee cannot be discussed or changed for this school.
Review what the school uses, show missing value or suggest a fitting plan, and respect its decision.
Tell the school that the SMS module is compulsory for everyone and cannot be removed from any plan.

questions.explanation: Understanding actual use and needs lets you offer real value or a better-fitting plan, while respecting the customer's choice.

questions.text: What should a good progress update to a school during onboarding include?

options.text: What is done, what comes next, and what the school must do.
Only good news, so that the school stays happy.
Technical details about our servers and databases.
A list of staff members who did not complete training.

questions.explanation: Clear updates show progress, next steps and shared responsibilities. Hiding problems or giving irrelevant details does not help.

questions.text: A headmaster complains that parents cannot see fee balances in the app. You find that the school has not yet entered the invoices. How do you respond?

options.text: Tell the headmaster that it is a system fault and promise a fix tomorrow.
Explain politely what is missing, show the steps to add the invoices, and offer to help.
Say it is the school's fault and end the conversation.
Enter the invoices yourself without telling the school.

questions.explanation: Honest, polite explanation with clear steps solves the problem and teaches the school. Blaming or making false promises damages trust.

description: Checks clear written and verbal communication at work, including listening, audience awareness and professional use of channels.

competencies.name: Clear Writing
competencies.description: Writing emails, notices and messages that are clear, correct and well organised.

competencies.name: Verbal and Phone Communication
competencies.description: Speaking clearly and confirming key details in calls and meetings.

competencies.name: Active Listening and Feedback
competencies.description: Listening carefully and giving and receiving feedback constructively.

competencies.name: Audience and Message Clarity
competencies.description: Adapting language and structure to the reader so that the message is understood and acted on.

competencies.name: Professional Etiquette and Channels
competencies.description: Choosing the right channel and keeping a professional tone and confidentiality.

questions.text: Which email subject line is the clearest?

options.text: Hello, please read this message when you have a moment
Urgent, please read this email as soon as possible
Term 2 fee report needed by Friday
Request for a meeting about some matters this term

questions.explanation: A clear subject line states the topic and the deadline, so the reader knows what to do.

questions.text: What is most important to check when you proofread a work message before sending it?

options.text: The number of emojis used in the message, and whether they match the topic being discussed.
Whether the message is long enough to look serious and important to a busy senior reader.
Names, numbers, dates and spelling, so that nothing misleads the reader.
Whether the message uses difficult words that make the writer look well educated.

questions.explanation: Wrong names, figures or dates can cause real mistakes, so check them carefully.

questions.text: You send a notice to staff, and three people reply with questions that show they misunderstood it. What is the best response?

options.text: Tell them to read messages more carefully next time, since the notice was clear enough already.
Send a short, simpler clarification and think about why the first message was unclear.
Ignore the questions because the notice was already sent and staff should check it again.
Answer each person privately, giving a slightly different explanation to suit their question.

questions.explanation: When several readers misunderstand, the message is probably unclear. A single clear clarification helps everyone and improves your next message.

questions.text: When speaking on the phone, what helps the other person to understand you?

options.text: Speaking quickly to save time and money, because the caller can always call back later.
Using many technical terms so that you sound professional and the caller trusts you.
Speaking in a very low voice so that other people in the office do not hear your call.
Speaking clearly at a moderate speed and spelling names or numbers when needed.

questions.explanation: Clear speech at a moderate speed, with names and numbers spelled out, avoids errors on a phone line.

questions.text: You phone a supplier to order 200 exercise books for delivery on Monday. What should you do at the end of the call?

options.text: Thank the supplier warmly and end the call quickly so that you do not waste airtime.
Assume the supplier will remember everything because it was said clearly on the phone.
Repeat the quantity, day and place of delivery to confirm them.
Ask the supplier to call you only if there is a problem with the order.

questions.explanation: Repeating the key details confirms that both sides understood. A short written confirmation afterwards is even better.

questions.text: Which behaviours show good listening? Select all that apply.

options.text: Looking at the speaker and giving your full attention.
Interrupting as soon as you think you know what will be said.
Asking questions when something is not clear.
Checking your phone while the other person is talking.
Summarising what you heard to confirm that you understood.

questions.explanation: Attention, clarifying questions and summarising are the main signs of good listening.

questions.text: Your supervisor says your reports are often late. You believe the delay is because another department sends data late. What is the best response?

options.text: Say the feedback is unfair and end the discussion.
Agree without comment and change nothing.
Complain about the other department to your colleagues.
Thank your supervisor, explain the data delay with an example, and suggest a solution.

questions.explanation: Receiving feedback well means listening, giving facts calmly and proposing a way forward, not defending or blaming.

questions.text: Before you write or speak, which question is most useful to ask yourself first?

options.text: How long can I make this message so that it looks complete and detailed?
Who is my audience, and what do they need to know or do?
How can I include everything that I know about the topic in one message?
How can I sound more impressive than the other writers in the office?

questions.explanation: Knowing the audience and the action you want helps you choose the right words, detail and structure.

questions.text: You must explain a new fee payment procedure to parents who mostly use basic phones and prefer Kiswahili. What is the best approach?

options.text: Use short, simple Kiswahili with clear steps by SMS, and offer to explain at school.
Send a long formal letter with detailed legal wording to every family through the pupils' bags.
Post a detailed notice in English on the school website and ask parents to read it there.
Ask teachers to explain it to parents in their own way when they meet them.

questions.explanation: The message should fit the audience's language and technology, and be simple with clear steps. The other options are hard for many parents to access or understand.

questions.text: Your message needs a decision from the director. What makes a quick and correct reply most likely?

options.text: Put the request at the end, after all the background.
Send several short messages, each with a different part of the request.
Put the decision needed and the deadline first, with the options if possible.
Mention the request lightly and hope the director asks questions.

questions.explanation: Busy readers act faster when the request, deadline and options appear at the start of the message.

questions.text: Which channel is most suitable for sending an official notice to a staff member?

options.text: A formal letter or email addressed to that person.
A WhatsApp status update that is visible to all of your contacts.
A voice note sent in a large group chat with other staff.
A message passed through a friend of the staff member.

questions.explanation: Official notices need a formal, traceable channel addressed to the person concerned.

questions.text: You post a message with confidential staff information in a parents' WhatsApp group by mistake. What should you do?

options.text: Say nothing and hope that no one has read it.
Ask members to ignore it but leave the message visible.
Delete it for everyone if possible, inform your supervisor at once, and apologise briefly.
Leave the group without telling anyone.

questions.explanation: Act quickly to limit the harm, and be honest with your supervisor so that the situation can be managed properly.

description: Checks whether the candidate can structure workplace reports, write summaries, use accurate evidence, make recommendations and record minutes.

competencies.name: Report Structure and Format
competencies.description: Organising a report logically with clear headings and the right place for detail.

competencies.name: Executive Summary and Clarity
competencies.description: Summarising key findings for busy readers in clear, plain language.

competencies.name: Evidence and Accuracy
competencies.description: Using checked data and sources and separating facts from opinion.

competencies.name: Conclusions and Recommendations
competencies.description: Making specific, practical recommendations that follow from the findings.

competencies.name: Minutes and Meeting Records
competencies.description: Recording decisions, actions, owners and deadlines accurately.

questions.text: Which order is commonly used for a workplace report?

options.text: Recommendations, title, conclusion, introduction, and then the findings at the very end.
Findings, references, title, introduction, and then conclusions in the last section.
Conclusions, appendix, title, findings, and then the introduction after the findings.
Title, introduction or purpose, findings, conclusions, recommendations.

questions.explanation: A logical flow from purpose to findings to conclusions and recommendations helps the reader to follow the argument.

questions.text: What is an executive summary?

options.text: A short opening section giving the main findings and recommendations for busy readers.
A list of all the books, articles and websites that the writer used while preparing the report.
The longest section of the report, which contains every data table and chart in full detail.
A copy of the meeting agenda that is attached to the front of the report.

questions.explanation: An executive summary lets a busy reader understand the key points and decisions needed without reading the full report.

questions.text: Which content is best for an executive summary?

options.text: Detailed raw data tables from all twelve months, so that readers can check every single figure.
Long acknowledgements and the history of the organisation, starting from its founding year.
The purpose, key findings and main recommendations, in about one page or less.
New information that does not appear anywhere else in the report, to surprise the reader.

questions.explanation: A good summary is short and covers purpose, findings and recommendations. Raw data and new information belong elsewhere.

questions.text: The school owner has only five minutes to read your 20-page report on fee collection. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the owner to find more time and read all 20 pages, because every detail matters.
Remove all figures and tables so that the report looks shorter and is easier to read quickly.
Send only the appendix, because it contains all the data that the owner needs to see.
Add a one-page summary at the front with key figures and recommended actions.

questions.explanation: A short summary at the front respects the reader's time and highlights what matters most.

questions.text: Why should a report state the source of its data?

options.text: So that readers can check the information and trust it.
So that the report looks longer and more serious.
So that the writer can avoid being asked questions.
So that the report can be printed on more pages.

questions.explanation: Stating sources makes the report credible and lets others verify the facts.

questions.text: While writing a report on attendance, you find that two registers give different totals for the same class. What should you do?

options.text: Use the higher number because it looks better for the school and nobody will ask for proof.
Take the average of the two numbers and use it without telling anyone how you got it.
Check the original records, find the correct figure, and note any uncertainty.
Leave that class out of the report without explanation, since the totals do not agree.

questions.explanation: Accuracy and honesty require checking the source and being open about any doubt. Hiding or guessing damages trust in the report.

questions.text: Which practices make the findings of a report more reliable? Select all that apply.

options.text: Separating facts from opinions.
Using only the data that supports your preferred conclusion.
Checking figures and totals before submitting.
Giving dates and sources of the data.
Rounding all figures upward.

questions.explanation: Separating facts from opinion, checking figures and naming sources make a report reliable. Selective data and biased rounding mislead readers.

questions.text: Which description fits a good recommendation?

options.text: General and broad, such as 'improve everything' or 'do better next year'.
Written before the findings are known, so that it can be sent early.
Based mainly on the personal feelings and opinions of the writer.
Specific, practical, and clearly linked to the findings.

questions.explanation: Good recommendations say what to do, who should do it, and why, based on the evidence.

questions.text: Your report finds that many fee arrears come from parents who never received payment instructions. Which recommendation is best?

options.text: Tell parents in a letter that they must pay on time and warn them about late payment penalties.
Say that further research is needed before anything can be done about the arrears this year.
Send payment instructions by SMS with every invoice, and review arrears after one term.
Increase school fees by ten percent next year to cover the arrears that remain unpaid.

questions.explanation: This recommendation is specific, solves the cause that was found, and includes a review. The others do not address the cause.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of the minutes of a meeting?

options.text: To record every word that each person said.
To record decisions, actions, who is responsible and deadlines.
To show who spoke the most during the meeting.
To replace the agenda of the next meeting.

questions.explanation: Minutes are a short official record of decisions and actions, so that people know what was agreed and who must do what.

questions.text: You are taking minutes. The committee agrees that the bursar will present the draft budget at the next meeting. How should you record this?

options.text: The committee talked about the draft budget for a long time and then moved on to other matters.
Resolved: the bursar will present the draft budget at the next meeting. Action: Bursar.
Many different opinions were given about the budget, and members agreed to think about it further.
The bursar is good at preparing budgets and was praised by several members of the committee.

questions.explanation: Minutes should state the decision and the person responsible, not the length of discussion or opinions.

questions.text: Your 12-page report is difficult to read, and readers cannot find information quickly. What is the best improvement?

options.text: Use a smaller font so that the report becomes shorter.
Remove the headings to make it look continuous.
Use clear headings, numbered sections, and short paragraphs.
Move all the findings to the end of the report.

questions.explanation: Headings, numbering and short paragraphs help readers to find and understand information quickly.

description: Checks whether the candidate can define scope, schedule work, manage risks and stakeholders, track progress and close projects.

competencies.name: Scope and Planning
competencies.description: Defining objectives and scope and controlling changes.

competencies.name: Scheduling and Resources
competencies.description: Sequencing tasks, understanding dependencies and managing time.

competencies.name: Risk Management
competencies.description: Identifying, assessing and responding to risks before they harm the project.

competencies.name: Stakeholder Management
competencies.description: Identifying and communicating with people affected by the project.

competencies.name: Monitoring and Closing
competencies.description: Tracking progress against the plan and closing projects with sign-off and lessons learned.

questions.text: Which of these is a project?

options.text: Cleaning the classrooms every morning before the pupils arrive, as a routine duty.
Running the monthly payroll for all staff, which is repeated in the same way each month.
Answering parents' calls every day, which continues as long as the school operates.
Launching a new fee system at a school, with a clear start and end date.

questions.explanation: A project is temporary, has a start and end, and creates a unique result. Daily or monthly routines are operations.

questions.text: What is 'scope creep'?

options.text: A project finishing earlier than planned because the team worked very hard on it.
Uncontrolled additions to the project scope without adjusting time or cost.
A delay caused by bad weather, power cuts or other events outside the team's control.
The project team getting smaller over time as members leave for other work or study.

questions.explanation: Scope creep happens when extra work is added informally, which often causes delays and extra cost.

questions.text: Halfway through a school software installation, the headmaster asks for three new features that were not agreed. What is the best action?

options.text: Add them quietly to keep the headmaster happy and to protect your working relationship.
Refuse every request for changes until the project is completely finished, whatever the reason.
Check the effect on time and cost, then agree a formal change before starting.
Stop the project until the headmaster decides everything that he wants in the system.

questions.explanation: Changes should be assessed and agreed formally, so that time, cost and expectations stay under control.

questions.text: Which tool shows project tasks, their durations and their dependencies over time?

options.text: A balance sheet.
A Gantt chart.
An organisation chart.
A pie chart of expenses.

questions.explanation: A Gantt chart displays tasks along a timeline and shows how they depend on each other.

questions.text: What is the critical path of a project?

options.text: The most expensive tasks in the project, which need the most careful approval.
The tasks that the project manager likes best and wants to supervise personally.
The shortest list of tasks that can safely be skipped if the project runs late.
The longest chain of dependent tasks, which sets the earliest finish date.

questions.explanation: Any delay on the critical path delays the whole project, so these tasks need the closest attention.

questions.text: In your rollout plan, training cannot start until the data import is done. The import is three days late. What should you do?

options.text: Check the effect on the schedule, tell stakeholders, and look for ways to recover time.
Start training anyway with an empty system and add the real data after the first sessions.
Ignore the delay because it is only three days and the team can surely absorb it later on.
Cancel all the training sessions and ask the school to wait until the data is finally ready.

questions.explanation: A delay in a dependent task can move later dates, so assess the effect, communicate, and plan recovery.

questions.text: What is a risk in project management?

options.text: A problem that has already happened and must now be solved by the team.
A mistake made by the team leader during the planning of the project.
An uncertain event that could affect the project objectives.
The total budget of the project, including the money kept for emergencies.

questions.explanation: A risk is something that might happen. Once it happens, it becomes an issue.

questions.text: A project to move five schools to new software has the risk 'key staff may be absent during go-live'. Which responses reduce this risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Train a backup person for each key role.
Ignore the risk until it happens.
Plan go-live outside exam and holiday periods.
Record the risk, give it an owner, and review it regularly.
Remove it from the list so that the team does not worry.

questions.explanation: Backups, better timing and active ownership all reduce the chance or effect of the risk. Ignoring or hiding it does not.

questions.text: Who is a stakeholder of a project?

options.text: Only the person who pays for the project and approves its budget.
Anyone who is affected by the project or can influence it.
Only the project team members who do the daily work on the tasks.
Only the people who will use the final product after it is delivered.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders include sponsors, users, staff, parents and others who are affected by or can influence the project.

questions.text: A teacher representative opposes your timetable system project because she was not told about changes. What is the best action?

options.text: Ignore her because she is not a manager.
Ask the headmaster to remove her from the committee.
Meet her, listen to her concerns, explain the plan, and agree how she will be informed.
Send her the full technical document by email.

questions.explanation: Engaging an unhappy stakeholder, listening, and agreeing regular communication turns opposition into support.

questions.text: Which is a useful way to track project progress?

options.text: Asking team members how they feel about the project.
Comparing planned progress with actual progress at regular status meetings.
Waiting until the final deadline to check the work.
Counting the number of emails sent about the project.

questions.explanation: Regular comparison of plan and actual progress shows problems early, while there is still time to act.

questions.text: The school is now using the new system, and the project work is complete. Which closing activity is most important?

options.text: Delete all project documents to save storage space.
Start another project immediately without any review.
Stop communicating with the school.
Hold a lessons-learned review, hand over documents, and get formal sign-off.

questions.explanation: Closing includes formal acceptance, a handover of documents, and learning for future projects.

description: Checks leadership judgment in setting direction, acting with integrity, motivating people, making decisions and leading change.

competencies.name: Vision and Direction
competencies.description: Setting a clear direction and linking daily work to goals.

competencies.name: Integrity and Accountability
competencies.description: Leading by example, admitting mistakes and handling conflicts of interest honestly.

competencies.name: Motivating and Developing People
competencies.description: Inspiring, delegating to and growing team members.

competencies.name: Decision Making
competencies.description: Making fair, well-informed and timely decisions.

competencies.name: Leading Change
competencies.description: Guiding people through change and resolving tensions in the team.

questions.text: What is a vision for a school or a team?

options.text: A clear picture of the future that the group wants to achieve.
A list of the rules and procedures that all staff must follow every day.
A report of last year's results and the lessons that were learned from them.
A timetable for the next week showing who teaches or works in each place.

questions.explanation: A vision describes the desired future and gives people a common direction.

questions.text: Your team is busy with daily tasks and has lost sight of why their work matters. What should you do?

options.text: Add more tasks to their daily schedule so that they have no time to think about problems.
Link their daily tasks to the team goals and explain the purpose clearly.
Wait until the team asks for direction before you say anything about the goals.
Tell the team to work harder and reward the fastest workers without explanation.

questions.explanation: People work with more energy when they understand how their tasks support a larger goal.

questions.text: Which example best describes leading by example?

options.text: Giving orders and checking that everyone obeys them without asking questions.
Asking staff to follow rules that you are too senior to follow yourself.
Arriving on time yourself when you ask staff to be punctual.
Telling stories about how well you worked in your previous school.

questions.explanation: Leaders earn trust when their own behaviour matches what they ask of others.

questions.text: You find a mistake you made in a report that already went to the board. No one has noticed it. What should you do?

options.text: Say nothing because the board will probably never notice such a small mistake in the report.
Quietly replace the file on the shared drive without telling anyone that it was changed.
Blame a junior staff member who helped you for the error, if somebody asks about it.
Tell the board, send the correction, and explain how you will avoid the error again.

questions.explanation: Accountability means admitting and correcting your own errors openly. This builds trust.

questions.text: A friend applies for a job in your department, and you are on the interview panel. What is the right action?

options.text: Declare the relationship and step aside from that selection decision.
Interview your friend but give scores without telling anyone about the friendship.
Tell your friend the interview questions in advance to be fair.
Say nothing because you are sure you can be objective.

questions.explanation: A conflict of interest must be declared, and the person should not take part in the decision, to keep the process fair.

questions.text: Which action most improves the motivation of a team member?

options.text: Increasing the workload to show trust.
Criticising mistakes in front of the whole team.
Giving clear goals, recognising good work, and offering chances to learn and grow.
Giving the same feedback to everyone, whatever they do.

questions.explanation: Clear goals, recognition and growth opportunities are strong, lasting motivators.

questions.text: A talented new teacher lacks confidence and avoids leading activities. What is the best leadership action?

options.text: Give a large responsibility without any support so that the teacher learns fast.
Wait until the teacher asks for more responsibility, however long that takes.
Tell the teacher to stop being shy and to speak up in front of colleagues.
Give small responsibilities with support, feedback, and encouragement.

questions.explanation: Gradual responsibility with support builds confidence and skills.

questions.text: Which behaviours show good delegation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Explaining the task, the expected result, and the deadline.
Giving the task and then disappearing without support.
Giving the person the authority needed to do the task.
Checking progress without taking the task back.
Delegating only the tasks that you dislike.

questions.explanation: Good delegation gives clarity, authority and follow-up while leaving the person responsible for doing the work.

questions.text: What should come first when you make a decision?

options.text: Choose the option that is the cheapest for the school this year.
Ask the most senior person in the room what they prefer.
Announce your decision to the staff before anyone can object.
Define the problem clearly and gather the facts.

questions.explanation: Good decisions start with a clear problem and reliable facts.

questions.text: A parent makes a serious complaint about a teacher. You have heard only the parent's side. What should you do?

options.text: Dismiss the teacher at once to protect the school.
Tell the parent that teachers are always right.
Listen to the teacher, collect facts, follow school procedures, then decide fairly.
Ignore the complaint until the parent complains again.

questions.explanation: A fair leader hears both sides and uses a proper procedure before deciding.

questions.text: What is the best first step when introducing a big change, such as a new school system?

options.text: Announce it suddenly so that no one has time to resist.
Explain why the change is needed and involve staff early.
Wait until the old system fails completely.
Introduce it first to the staff who like change and ignore others.

questions.explanation: People accept change more easily when they understand the reason and have a voice in how it happens.

questions.text: Two senior teachers argue regularly and the staff room is tense. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore it until they stop by themselves.
Support the teacher that you like more.
Move one of them to another block without discussion.
Meet them separately and then together, focus on the issues, and agree on solutions.

questions.explanation: Leaders address conflict early, listen to both sides, and focus on issues rather than personalities.

description: Checks practical team-management skills: delegation, coaching, performance conversations, conflict resolution, motivation and meetings.

competencies.name: Delegation and Work Allocation
competencies.description: Giving tasks, authority and support to the right people.

competencies.name: Coaching and Feedback
competencies.description: Helping people to improve through clear, constructive feedback and guidance.

competencies.name: Performance Management
competencies.description: Setting clear goals and holding fair, specific performance conversations.

competencies.name: Conflict Resolution
competencies.description: Handling disagreements fairly and early, and finding solutions that last.

competencies.name: Motivation and Running Meetings
competencies.description: Recognising effort and leading meetings that produce decisions and actions.

questions.text: What is delegation?

options.text: Doing all the important work yourself so that it is always done to your own standard.
Giving someone a task and the authority to do it, while you stay accountable.
Telling someone to do a task and blaming them completely if the result is poor.
Sharing your personal problems with your team members so that they understand you better.

questions.explanation: Delegation passes the task and authority to another person, but the manager is still accountable for the outcome.

questions.text: You have a large report to complete. A team member has the skills but little experience. What should you do?

options.text: Give clear instructions, a deadline and support, and let the member do part of it.
Do the whole report yourself, to avoid mistakes and to be sure of meeting the deadline.
Give the member only the hardest part of the report and offer no help along the way.
Give the task without instructions so that they learn alone by finding their own way.

questions.explanation: Clear instructions and support let a developing team member succeed and grow.

questions.text: Which is an example of constructive feedback?

options.text: 'You are always so careless with your work, and I am tired of correcting your mistakes every week.'
'Your report is simply bad, and it is far below the standard that we expect in this office.'
'The totals in your last report did not match the table. Please recheck; I can show you how.'
'Some people say that your report is poor, so you should try to do much better next time.'

questions.explanation: Constructive feedback is specific, focused on the work, and offers help to improve.

questions.text: A new staff member makes the same data-entry mistake for the third time. What is the best coaching approach?

options.text: Send a formal warning letter at once and place a copy of it in the staff member's file.
Remind them in front of the whole team to be more careful with the data they enter.
Move the task to another person without explanation, and give the new staff member other work.
Sit with them, show the correct method, let them practise, and agree on a check.

questions.explanation: Coaching combines demonstration, practice and follow-up. Punishment or public correction does not teach the skill.

questions.text: In goal setting, what do the letters in SMART goals stand for?

options.text: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound
Simple, Manageable, Action-oriented, Realistic, Timetabled
Strategic, Meaningful, Ambitious, Rewarding, Time-limited
Specific, Minimal, Agreed, Random, Timed

questions.explanation: SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound, which makes them clear and trackable.

questions.text: A staff member's performance has dropped over the last two months. What should you do first?

options.text: Give a formal written warning immediately and send a copy to the head office for the file.
Talk privately to understand the reasons, share examples, and agree support and targets.
Discuss the matter openly in the next team meeting so that every colleague can give their views on it.
Wait for the annual appraisal and then discuss the drop in performance with the staff member.

questions.explanation: A private, fact-based conversation finds the cause and agrees a plan. Public or delayed action is unfair and less effective.

questions.text: Which should be included in a good performance conversation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Specific examples of results or behaviour.
Comparison with a named colleague.
Listening to the employee's point of view.
Agreed next steps and a follow-up date.
Criticism of the employee's personal character.

questions.explanation: Good conversations are specific, two-way and end with agreed actions. Comparisons and personal attacks harm trust.

questions.text: Which approach to conflict aims to find a solution that satisfies both sides?

options.text: Avoiding, where the issue is never discussed and both sides simply move on.
Competing, where one side must win and the other side has to accept the result.
Collaborating, where both sides work together to solve the problem.
Giving in, where one side always accepts the other's demand to keep the peace.

questions.explanation: Collaborating looks for a solution that meets the needs of both parties and keeps the relationship.

questions.text: Two team members each complain about the other to you separately and each wants you to take their side. What should you do?

options.text: Agree with the one who complained first.
Tell them to solve it alone without your involvement.
Move one of them to a different team immediately.
Listen to both, stay neutral, then bring them together to agree on a solution.

questions.explanation: Neutral listening followed by a joint conversation treats both fairly and aims at a lasting solution.

questions.text: Which is a good way to recognise a team member's effort?

options.text: Give no feedback so that the person does not become proud or expect a reward.
Praise only the person who already receives the most praise from the manager.
Mention their effort only in the yearly review, together with their other results.
Thank them specifically for what they did and how it helped.

questions.explanation: Specific and timely recognition motivates people and shows what good work looks like.

questions.text: What makes a team meeting effective?

options.text: A long discussion without a fixed end time.
A clear agenda, a start and an end on time, and recorded actions.
Inviting everyone in the school whether or not it concerns them.
Having the leader speak for most of the time.

questions.explanation: An agenda, time discipline and recorded actions make meetings productive.

questions.text: In your weekly meeting, one person talks most of the time and others stay silent. What should you do?

options.text: Allow it because the talkative person knows the most.
Stop holding meetings and send messages instead.
Ask the quiet members by name for their ideas and set time limits for speakers.
Tell the quiet members they must speak more or leave.

questions.explanation: Inviting quiet members and managing speaking time gives everyone a voice and improves decisions.

description: Checks whether the candidate can set goals, analyse the situation, choose KPIs, allocate resources and review progress against a plan.

competencies.name: Vision, Mission and Goals
competencies.description: Defining purpose, direction and clear goals.

competencies.name: Situation Analysis
competencies.description: Using tools such as SWOT to understand internal and external factors.

competencies.name: KPIs and Measurement
competencies.description: Choosing measurable indicators that show progress toward goals.

competencies.name: Resource Allocation and Action Planning
competencies.description: Linking budget, people and time to strategic priorities.

competencies.name: Monitoring and Review
competencies.description: Reviewing progress regularly and adjusting the plan when conditions change.

questions.text: What does a mission statement describe?

options.text: The future position that the organisation hopes to reach in ten years.
The yearly budget of the organisation.
Why the organisation exists, what it does, and who it serves.
The list of staff and their job titles.

questions.explanation: A mission states the purpose of the organisation. The future picture is the vision.

questions.text: Which is the best-written school goal?

options.text: Improve the results in all subjects and in all classes as much as we possibly can.
Have a good school that parents are proud of and that is respected in the region.
Do better than other schools in the district in every examination that we sit.
Raise the Standard Seven pass rate from 70% to 80% by the end of next year.

questions.explanation: A good goal is specific, measurable and has a deadline.

questions.text: The board wants the school to become 'the best in the region' but has not said how this will be measured. What should you do?

options.text: Accept the statement as it is, because it is inspiring and will motivate the staff.
Help the board to turn it into specific, measurable goals with deadlines.
Wait until the end of the year to decide how the school's progress should be measured.
Choose the measure that makes the school look best to parents and visitors.

questions.explanation: Broad ambitions need measurable goals and dates, so that progress can be checked.

questions.text: What does SWOT stand for?

options.text: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats
Standards, Workloads, Objectives, Time-schedules
Skills, Salaries, Outcomes, Time-management
Strategy, Wealth, Operations, Training-needs

questions.explanation: SWOT analysis looks at internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats.

questions.text: In a SWOT analysis of a school, a new competing school opening nearby is best classified as which?

options.text: A strength
An opportunity
A weakness
A threat

questions.explanation: It is an external factor that could harm the school, so it is a threat.

questions.text: Staff are listing items for a SWOT analysis of your school. Which one is an internal weakness?

options.text: Many teachers have not been trained to use computers.
The government starts a new support programme for schools.
The cost of electricity is rising across the country.
The school has a strong reputation in the community.

questions.explanation: Weaknesses are internal factors that the school can improve, such as staff skills. The others are external or strengths.

questions.text: What is a KPI?

options.text: A list of the problems that staff have reported to the management this term.
A yearly party that is held for all the staff to celebrate the end of the school year.
A measurable value that shows how well a key objective is being achieved.
A document that shows the school's rules and the penalties for breaking them.

questions.explanation: KPI means key performance indicator, a number used to track progress toward an objective.

questions.text: A school wants to improve fee collection. Which would be good KPIs? Select all that apply.

options.text: Percentage of fees collected by the due date.
Number of staff members in the office.
Total fee arrears at the end of each term.
Number of posters on the notice board.
Average number of days parents take to pay after the invoice.

questions.explanation: These indicators directly measure fee collection performance. Staff numbers and posters do not.

questions.text: Why should the budget be linked to the strategic priorities?

options.text: So that every department receives exactly the same amount, whatever its role in the plan.
So that limited money and staff time go to the activities that best support goals.
So that the budget never has to change during the year, even if the situation changes.
So that spending on every plan activity needs no approval from the head or the board.

questions.explanation: Resources are limited, so they should support the most important goals.

questions.text: Your school can afford only one of three projects: a computer lab, a new library roof, or a school bus. How should you decide?

options.text: Divide the money equally among the three projects.
Choose the cheapest one to save the most money.
Rank them against the plan's priorities using criteria such as impact, urgency and cost.
Choose the project that the loudest staff member wants.

questions.explanation: Prioritising with clear criteria linked to the strategy leads to fair, defensible decisions.

questions.text: Why should a strategic plan be reviewed regularly?

options.text: To replace the vision every term.
To show that the plan cannot be changed.
To check progress, learn from results, and adjust to changes.
To find staff to blame.

questions.explanation: Regular reviews show whether the plan is working and allow corrections when conditions change.

questions.text: At the mid-year review, most targets are behind because the plan assumed a grant that was never received. What should you do?

options.text: Continue unchanged and hope that the grant arrives.
Hide the results from the board until the end of the year.
Blame the staff for not working hard enough.
Identify the cause, revise the targets and priorities, and tell stakeholders.

questions.explanation: A plan must be adjusted when a key assumption fails. Honest review and communication keep the plan realistic.
